messages.subject: Re: [codex_wes_cnv] [qustion about the number of FP reported in the CODEX manuscript]
messages.subject_clean: [codex_wes_cnv] [qustion about the number of FP reported in the CODEX manuscript]
messages.body_plain:
I did not apply any filtering on the calls. You need to wisely choose the number of latent factors. This will result in different number of CNV calls. Also quality control procedures are very important too and can potentially remove false positives. I used the bed file downloaded from the 1000 Genomes Project.

Also bear in mind, the bam files you downloaded from the 1000 Genomes Project have been changing and this can be also one factor although I don’t think this will lead to too much a difference.

Hope this is helpful to you.

Yuchao

> On Sep 3, 2017, at 4:53 AM, Tomasz Gambin <tga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Yuchao,
>
> I have one more question about CODEX parameters.
> Recently I tried to run CODEX on 90 samples from 1000 genomes project that you used in your manuscript.
>
> When I run CODEX with parameters defined in vignette:
> https://github.com/yuchaojiang/CODEX/blob/master/package/vignettes/CODEX_vignettes.Rnw
> I got many more calls than you , e.g. >1800 CNVs just for chr1, when you had 361.
> I also noticed my calls have much higher mBIC than those reported in manuscript.
>
> I wander what parameters you used to obtain more stringent results. Did you perform any additional filtering ?
>
> Thanks,
> Tomek
>
>

> > >
> > > This is correct. Essentially not all 1806 calls by CODEX overlap with HapMap CNV calls, same with other three methods too. We treat HapMap CNV calls as gold standards -- the ones called by CODEX that don't overlap with the gold standards cannot be categorized as FP, TP, TN, or FN. This has been a long time, but what we did should be: (1) first filter out all CODEX, XHMM, etc.'s  calls that don't overlap with any HapMap calls, (2) for those that do overlap, we attribute them to FP, TP, TN, or FN and then calculate the precision and recall.
> > >
> > > To filtering on the gold standard CNV calls we have include: (1) overlap with at least 2 and at most 20 exons. (2) with NA rates less than 5% (some samples have NA from HapMap microarray calls) (3) number of CNV states <=3 (4) CNV rate less than 90% with at least one non-null sample (since we only have 90 samples, for some microarray calls from all cohort the 90 samples are all copy-number-neutral); (5) not overlap with previously reported seg dup region.

messages.subject: How to plot log(Y / λ) ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been trying CODEX for CNV calling and I have got pretty good results so far. For visual validation, I would like to generate log(Y / λ) plots like you have done in the manuscript for ATRX gene. Is there a function in CODEX for this purpose? Can you please help?

Thank you,
Bekir

messages.subject: Re: [codex_wes_cnv] How to plot log(Y / λ) ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bekir,

Glad CODEX is running well for you. We draw the plot for ATRX region in our paper using R from scratch. Each black line is a normalized log ratio over the region for one sample. The red regions are where CNVs are detected. I don't have the code any more and even if I do it will not be very generalized at all.

Y is the raw depth of coverage and this should be Y_qc in your code.
lambda is the expected depth of coverage if there is no CNVs. This is Yhat[[optK]] in your code.

You can take the log ratio of these two matrices and it will return a matrix (exons x samples or vice versa). You can then zoon into a region and plot for each sample. start(ref_qc) and end(ref_qc) give you the starting and ending positions for your exonic targets after QC.

I hope this is of help to you. Alternatively, you can load your results in IGV for direct visualization without the need for coding the script yourself. Refer to the section "Visualization by IGV" in our GitHub page here. https://github.com/yuchaojiang/CODEX

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.subject: questions about targeted sequencing results
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm new to CNV analysis, and am trying to use Codex to analyze germline copy number variation in a targeted sequencing experiment looking at ~1000 genes or small intergenic regions. Most of the genes are OR genes, which are known to have a lot of variation in copy number. My sample includes 150 individuals from six populations. I have been following the code posted on Github for targeted sequencing. I have one quick question and then a more involved question--

1. Is the following set of commands in targeted sequencing one you recommend for general use for further QC of samples or is that just for the example dataset?
> sampfilter=apply(Y_qc,2,median)>=50   # need to exclude 3 samples (exon capture failure)
> sampname_qc=sampname_qc[sampfilter]
> Y_qc=Y_qc[,sampfilter]

2. I am able to get the program to run successfully, but I'm having trouble with the segmentation step. When I source the 'segment_targeted.R' script and run the For loop to make the finalcall file, the finalcall file ends up being one row of NA (see below). Does that mean the program is finding no copy number variation in my data? The optimal K is estimated at 13, but I get the same result if I make K lower (such as K=2).

> dim(Y_qc)
[1] 809 121
> length(ref_qc)
[1] 809
> length(sampname_qc)
[1] 121
> dim(Yhat[[2]])
[1] 809 121
> length(chr_qc)
[1] 809
> optK=2
> finalcall=matrix(ncol=14)
> colnames(finalcall)=c('sample_name','chr','gene','cnv',
+                       'st_bp','ed_bp','length_kb',
+                       'st_exon','ed_exon','raw_cov',

When I do that, I get around 300 total deletions/duplications across 112 individuals (1-5 deletions/duplications per individual). However, some of the regions seem really long and a few "cross" chromosomes, which I'm guessing is because of the data is from targeted sequencing and not whole exome.

Hi Carrie,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. Please see my reply below. Hope it is of help!

Yuchao

> On Sep 29, 2017, at 1:35 PM, carrie.c...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I'm new to CNV analysis, and am trying to use Codex to analyze germline copy number variation in a targeted sequencing experiment looking at ~1000 genes or small intergenic regions. Most of the genes are OR genes, which are known to have a lot of variation in copy number. My sample includes 150 individuals from six populations. I have been following the code posted on Github for targeted sequencing. I have one quick question and then a more involved question--
>
> 1. Is the following set of commands in targeted sequencing one you recommend for general use for further QC of samples or is that just for the example dataset?
> > sampfilter=apply(Y_qc,2,median)>=50   # need to exclude 3 samples (exon capture failure)
> > sampname_qc=sampname_qc[sampfilter]
> > Y_qc=Y_qc[,sampfilter]
>

This is used for one dataset that I analyzed, which requires the median read depth across all targets for a sample to be greater than 50. Sometimes the library prep failed for certain samples and this QC is used to remove these samples. You can of course relax this or make this more stringent depending on your experimental design and sequencing depth.

> 2. I am able to get the program to run successfully, but I'm having trouble with the segmentation step. When I source the 'segment_targeted.R' script and run the For loop to make the finalcall file, the finalcall file ends up being one row of NA (see below). Does that mean the program is finding no copy number variation in my data? The optimal K is estimated at 13, but I get the same result if I make K lower (such as K=2).
>
> > dim(Y_qc)
> [1] 809 121
> > length(ref_qc)
> [1] 809
> > length(sampname_qc)
> [1] 121
> > dim(Yhat[[2]])
> [1] 809 121
> > length(chr_qc)
> [1] 809
> > optK=2
> > finalcall=matrix(ncol=14)
> > colnames(finalcall)=c('sample_name','chr','gene','cnv',
> +                       'st_bp','ed_bp','length_kb',
> +                       'st_exon','ed_exon','raw_cov',
> +                       'norm_cov','copy_no','lratio',
> +                       'mBIC')
> > for(genei in unique(gene_qc)){
> + cat('Segmenting gene',genei,'\n')
> + geneindex=which(gene_qc==genei)
> + yi=Y_qc[geneindex,]
> + yhati=Yhat[[optK]][geneindex,]
> + refi=ref_qc[geneindex]
> + chri=chr_qc[geneindex][1]
> + finalcalli=segment_targeted(yi, yhati, sampname_qc, refi, genei, chri, lmax=length(geneindex), mode='integer')
> + finalcall=rbind(finalcall,finalcalli)
> + }
> Segmenting gene OR4G4P
> Segmenting gene OR4G11P
> ...
> Segmenting gene OR2AF1P
> Segmenting gene OR3B1P
> > finalcall
>      sample_name chr gene cnv st_bp ed_bp length_kb st_exon ed_exon raw_cov
> [1,] NA          NA  NA   NA  NA    NA    NA        NA      NA      NA
>      norm_cov copy_no lratio mBIC
> [1,] NA       NA      NA     NA
>
> I tried using the finalcall commands in the Bioconductor vignette instead of the targeted sequencing ones to see what happens (with optK = 13)-
> > finalcall <- segment(Y_qc, Yhat, optK = optK, K = K, sampname_qc, ref_qc, chr, lmax = 200, mode = "integer")
> When I do that, I get around 300 total deletions/duplications across 112 individuals (1-5 deletions/duplications per individual). However, some of the regions seem really long and a few "cross" chromosomes, which I'm guessing is because of the data is from targeted sequencing and not whole exome.
>
> Do you have any suggestions on how I should proceed? Could I be doing something wrong with the segmentation step in the targeted selection protocol? Or is the 0 deletions/duplications result valid?
>

I think your number of latent factors is chosen to high (opt =13 currently). This will remove most of your CNV signals as latent artifacts or batch effects. You can refer to the pdf generated in the choiceofK() step however it can be sometimes not indicative of an optimal value. If this is the case, I still would recommend a smaller optK — we rarely set this value to be greater than 10 in our analysis (usually around 5). Also for your dataset, it seems that you have some positive controls, which you can use to guide the choice of optK (i.e., try different optK and see if the known CNV signals are retained without too many potential false positives).

> Thank you very much!
> Carrie
